_changelog: v1.0.1 (2026-10-16) cold-case model: added the caution that longer answers make each pass fetch more working memory, so the 18 ms pass time is re-measured, not assumed

v1.0.0 (2026-10-16) first version, from latent-season10-bible-v1.0.1.md row a10e02, writer brief a10e02-v1.0.0.md, LATENT catalog v1.0.73 and latent-syllabus-v1.0.3.md. a10e01's next field was honoured: a suspension bridge closed overnight for inspection, the two speeds of one card in plain words (reading the prompt and writing the answer), time to first token, the time between tokens, and throughput. Keeps apart from s9e08, a6e05 and a2e07 (no gateway, no streaming screen: here two speeds of one card and planning a job by them), from a10e09 (one job on one card, no routing), from s9e13 and s9e07 (the closure is only the deadline: no animals, no buses), and from a10e01's furnace (no kiln, oven or smelter). Shared given data: Llama 3.1 8B, 8.03 billion weights, 16.06 billion bytes in 16 bits, about 15 GB on the card's meter; one A100 80GB, 2,039 GB/s and 312 TFLOPS dense (16-bit); sizes in the meter's units (1 GB = 1,024 MB), speeds in the maker's (1,000). The contractor's own measurements, never a source's: reading runs at 10,000 tokens a second (a 2,000-token section in 0.2 s); the writing curve is 10 ms plus 0.25 ms per report in a pass, rounded in this case to whole ms (one report 10 ms, 4 reports 11, 8 reports 12, 32 reports 18). Arithmetic: the sheet 900 x 3,000 / 10,000 = 270 s; one section TTFT 0.21 s (reading plus the first pass) + 999 x 10 ms = 10.2 s; 900 x 10.2 = 9,180 s, 03:30 to 06:03; 5,400 / 10.2 = 529 at 05:00; grades 0.2 + 3 x 0.01 = 0.23 s, 207 s; 32 at once 18 ms a pass, 1,778 tokens a second, 28 groups of 32 and one of 4 in 695 s (11 min 35 s), done 03:41:35; twice the sums 9,090 s (06:01:30); 500-token notes 9,045 s (06:00:45, 135 s saved). Card time 9,180 s = 2.55 h, $7.11 at Lambda's list price of $2.79 a card hour (read 16 October 2026), against 695 s, $0.54. Timeline: the job has written one-word grades on every monthly closure since Tuesday 10 March 2026 (last on Tuesday 11 August, whose job log gave the 10,000); the owner signed the new contract on Tuesday 1 September, starting with tonight's closure; Hildebrand updated the plan sheet on Thursday 3 September; the bridge closed 22:00 Tuesday 8 September, inspection ended 03:20, job started 03:30 Wednesday 9 September, the sheet's finish 03:34:30; the job sends all reports in one file at the end; Kristiina walks the deck after the inspection and sits down to read at 05:00, finds no file and phones (the alert); 529 of 900 at 05:00; 705 at 05:30; the job ends 06:03; she reads the last watch report and the bridge reopens 06:20; the post at about 06:40. Cold case: 4 months later, 9 September 2026 to Friday 8 January 2027 (closures 13 October, 10 November, 8 December; the owner's December request for 2,000-token reports from the January closure; the update is posted before it). Standards note conditional, not legal advice. Sources read 16 October 2026.
title: Two Phases
setting: a suspension bridge closed overnight for inspection

post.author: u/night_lead_omolara
post.title: I lead the night inspection on a suspension bridge. The plan sheet said our new reports would take 4.5 minutes. At 05:00, half an hour before reopening, the bar said 529 of 900.

blocks.text: I'm Omolara, night lead for the inspection team on the Strathcarne Bridge, a suspension bridge: its road deck hangs from two great cables slung between towers. On the second Tuesday night of each month it closes, 22:00 to 05:30, for inspection.

Rope-access inspectors, hanging from ropes, and a drone check 900 numbered sections of deck and cable. Each section's notes and measurements come to about 2,000 tokens: the small pieces of text a language model reads and writes.
Since March our firm has run its own model on the notes: Llama 3.1 8B, a file of 8.03 billion learned numbers called weights, 16.06 billion bytes.
It runs on one graphics card we own, an NVIDIA A100 80GB: thousands of small adders, fed numbers along one fast memory road.
The maker lists the road at 2,039 GB, billions of bytes, a second. The adders do 312 trillion sums a second: 312 TFLOPS, short for trillion floating-point operations per second.
Each section is two jobs. First the card reads the notes, all 2,000 tokens in one pass, like taking in a letter at a glance. Reading waits on the adders: 0.2 s a section, our job log says.

Then it writes, one token per pass, like writing the reply one word at a time. Every pass fetches all 16.06 billion bytes along the road, so writing waits on the road: about 10 ms, a hundredth of a second, per token.
A pass can also serve several answers written side by side: it fetches the weights once and adds one token to each. Our script, the small program that feeds the card, sends one section at a time.
Engineers call the reading prefill and the writing decode.

Until tonight each section got a one-word grade, sound or watch: 0.23 s a section, about 3.5 minutes for all 900. Before reopening, the owner's bridge engineer, Kristiina, reads every section graded watch or worse.

On Tuesday 1 September the owner signed a new contract: from tonight, a full report of about 1,000 tokens per section, ready by reopening. The inspection ends at 03:20, so the job starts at 03:30. On Thursday 3 September our planner, Hildebrand, updated the plan sheet.

blocks.title: PLAN SHEET · Strathcarne night job
items: Tokens per section: 3,000 (2,000 of notes, 1,000 of report)
Speed: 10,000 tokens a second (measured, job log, 11 August)

blocks.text: The job started at 03:30; it sends every report in one file at the end. Kristiina walked the deck, then sat down to read at 05:00. No file. She phoned me. The progress bar said 529 of 900.
It added one section every ten seconds, steady as a slow count of the hanger cables.
Each job log line shows the time, the section, its reading, the wait for its first token, the gap between tokens, and the whole section.

04:59:55  section 530  reading 0.20 s  first token 0.21 s  then 10 ms a token

Bottom row, section 1 tonight: reading its notes until 0.2 seconds, then writing its report until 10.2 seconds. Markers at 0.3 seconds, the sheet's figure, and 10.2 seconds, section 1 done.

blocks.text: By hand: 900 × 10.2 s = 9,180 s, 2 h 33 min, so the job would end at 06:03, 33 minutes after reopening. Kristiina kept the bridge shut until she had read the last watch report. It reopened at 06:20, fifty minutes late.
Hildebrand says the sheet was measured, so the script must be broken. The next closure is Tuesday 13 October. What should we change?

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nothing on that bridge is haunted, though a bar that counts like a slow bell is grim. Your log already gives every section two clocks. The wait from sending a section until its first token arrives is its time to first token, TTFT for short. The gap between one token and the next is the inter-token latency, ITL. Two questions. Where in your log does 10,000 tokens a second appear, and what is the card doing at that moment? And how many tokens did each section write in August, against tonight?

replies.author: u/night_lead_omolara
replies.text: Only in the reading: 2,000 tokens in 0.2 s. The writing runs at one token every 10 ms, about 100 a second. In August each section wrote 3 tokens. Tonight, 1,000.

comments.author: u/ten_thousand_hildebrand
comments.text: I wrote the sheet. 10,000 tokens a second is the job's throughput, the tokens a second the card handles across all its work, and I took it from August's job log. Measured, not guessed. The sheet has matched every closure since March to within a minute. If tonight ran slower, the script is broken. And if the card really is short, buy one with twice the sums a second. A report is just more tokens.

replies.author: u/night_lead_omolara
replies.text: The script is the same file as in August. Only the report length changed.

replies.author: u/ten_thousand_hildebrand
replies.text: Then it's the card. More sums, more tokens.

comments.author: u/deck_notes_mahnoor
comments.text: Rope-access inspector here. Our notes are padded: every crack measured twice, the wind written on every line. Cut each section to its best 500 tokens and the card has a quarter as much to read. Less in, less to wait for.

replies.author: u/night_lead_omolara
replies.text: Reading took 0.2 s a section tonight. And the second measurement is how we catch a gauge slipping.

comments.author: u/bridge_engineer_kristiina
comments.text: The engineer who phoned. I won't open a bridge on reports I haven't read. Next month, give me the one-word grades overnight, as before; they took 3.5 minutes. I'll read the notes for every watch section myself, and your team can write the full reports in the day.

replies.author: u/night_lead_omolara
replies.text: The owner's contract asks for the reports by reopening. Written by day, they'd reach the owner hours late.

reply.prompt: It's 06:40 on Wednesday 9 September, and the next closure is Tuesday 13 October. What should the contractor change before then? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Time reading and writing apart, and send 32 sections at once.
options.part2: On Thursday Hildebrand rebuilt the sheet with two lines. Reading: 900 × 2,000 tokens at 10,000 a second, 180 s. Writing: 900,000 tokens at the writing speed. Then the script was set to send 32 sections at once. Each pass fetched the weights once and added a token to all 32 reports: 18 ms a pass on our own curve, 1,778 tokens a second. On Tuesday 13 October the job ran 28 groups of 32 and one of 4 and finished at 03:41:35, 11 min 35 s after it started, as the sim had said. Each report's first token now waited for its group's reading, up to 6.42 s, and nobody minded, because nobody watches a report being written. Kristiina sat down at 05:00 to a full file, had read every watch report by 05:20, and the bridge reopened at 05:30.
options.senior: Plan a generation job with two speeds, not one: prompt tokens at the reading speed (prefill, about 10,000 a second here) and answer tokens at the writing speed (decode, about 100 a second for one answer). Then use the cheap lever writing offers: one fetch of the weights serves every answer in the pass, so 32 answers take 18 ms instead of 10, and the card writes 1,778 tokens a second instead of 100. The cost is a longer first token for each answer, which a batch job can afford and a person waiting might not.

options.text: Move the job to a card with twice the sums a second of tonight's card.
options.part2: Hildebrand priced a card whose sheet shows twice the sums a second on the same 2,039 GB/s road. Before buying, I set it up in the sim. Reading fell from 0.2 s to 0.1 s a section. Writing stayed at 10 ms a token, because every pass still fetches 16.06 billion bytes along the same road. The job would end at 06:01:30 instead of 06:03, with 534 of 900 done at 05:00 instead of 529. We would have paid for a new card to save 90 seconds and still reopen late.
options.senior: Writing waits on the memory road, not the adders: each token fetches every weight, about one sum per byte, while the A100 could do about 153 sums per byte. More sums a second speed up only the reading, which was 3 of the 153 minutes. Before buying a card, ask which phase the job spends its time in and what limits that phase.

options.text: Grade every section tonight as before, and write full reports by day.
options.verdict: On time, but not as contracted
options.part2: On Tuesday 13 October the job wrote one-word grades again: 0.23 s a section, all 900 in 207 s, done at 03:33:27. Kristiina read the grades and the notes of every watch section, and the bridge reopened at 05:30. The day shift ran the full reports from 08:00, one at a time, and they reached the owner at 10:33, five hours after the contract asks. The owner's manager wrote that the contract says reports by reopening, and asked when that would start.
options.senior: It is an honest trade: the bridge opens on time because the grades are short, and the cost moves to the contract, which wanted the reports before reopening. It also leaves the planning error in place, so the next long job will be planned with the same wrong speed. Timing the two phases apart fixes both.

options.text: Trim each section's notes to 500 tokens so the card has less to read.
options.part2: Mahnoor's team cut every section's notes to 500 tokens. In the sim, reading fell from 0.2 s to 0.05 s a section. Writing stayed at 10 ms a token, 10 s a report. The job would end at 06:00:45, with 537 of 900 done at 05:00. We saved 135 seconds of 153 minutes, and lost the second measurements that catch a slipping gauge.
options.senior: Shortening the prompt trims the fast phase. Reading 2,000 tokens is one pass and took 0.2 s; writing 1,000 tokens is 1,000 passes and took 10 s. Find which phase holds the time before cutting anything, and never cut the evidence a report is built from to save the part that was already quick.

sim.title: Plan the night job with two clocks
sim.lede: You're Omolara at 03:20 on Wednesday 9 September, before the job starts. No real model runs here: every figure is worked out from given numbers. Given: 900 sections, each with 2,000 tokens of notes and a 1,000-token report; Llama 3.1 8B (16.06 billion bytes) on one A100 80GB (2,039 GB/s, 312 TFLOPS); the bridge reopens at 05:30. Two of the contractor's own measurements: reading runs at 10,000 tokens a second, 0.2 s a section; writing takes 10 ms a pass plus 0.25 ms for each report in it, rounded to whole ms (1 report: 10 ms, 8: 12 ms, 32: 18 ms). One pass adds one token to every report in it. Sending several sections at once makes a group: the card reads all the group's notes, then writes all its reports together. The other card is a what-if with twice the sums a second on the same road.
sim.tryThis: Try this: the opening plan is one at a time: TTFT 0.21 s, ITL 10 ms, 10.2 s a section, 9,180 s, ending 06:03:00, 529 done at 05:00, against the sheet's 270 s. Play the night. Set the report to 3 tokens: 207 s, as in August. Back to 1,000 and send 32 at once: 18 ms a pass, 1,778 tokens a second, done at 03:41:35, with the first token waiting up to 6.42 s. Pick the card with twice the sums: reading halves, writing does not move. Cut the notes to 500: 135 s saved. Then play each reply.

explain.oneLine: Nothing on the bridge was haunted. Each section was two jobs on one card at two speeds: reading 2,000 tokens of notes in one pass, 0.2 s (about 10,000 a second), then writing a 1,000-token report one token per pass, about 10 ms each (about 100 a second). The plan sheet timed all 3,000 tokens at the reading speed, 270 s. One at a time the job took 900 × 10.2 = 9,180 s and ended at 06:03; sent 32 at once, it takes 695 s.

steps.title: Reading the notes: one pass for all 2,000 tokens.
steps.text: First, the card fetches each weight once along the memory road. Then it uses that weight for all 2,000 tokens of the section's notes in the same pass, about 2 sums per weight for each token: 2 × 8.03 billion × 2,000 = 32 trillion sums. At the sheet's 312 trillion a second that would take 0.10 s; the contractor's job log measures 0.2 s, about half the sheet's rate, much as a10e01's foundry found. Reading waits on the adders, so it is math limited, and it runs at about 10,000 tokens a second. Engineers call it prefill. What can go wrong: a speed measured here looks like the card's speed for everything.

steps.title: Writing the report: one pass per token.
steps.text: First, the card fetches all 16.06 billion bytes of weights along the road. Second, its adders do about two sums per weight to choose the next token, about one sum per byte fetched. Third, it adds that token to the report, and repeats, 1,000 times. The road sets the floor: 16.06 ÷ 2,039 GB/s = 7.9 ms a token. The contractor's own writing curve is 10 ms plus 0.25 ms for each report in the pass; this case rounds one report's 10.25 ms to 10 ms, about 100 tokens a second. That is decode. It is memory limited: the A100's adders could do about 153 sums for each byte the road delivers (312 ÷ 2.039), and writing uses one. What can go wrong: a card with more sums a second leaves this step exactly as slow.

steps.title: Two clocks, and the sum the sheet skipped.
steps.text: Time to first token (TTFT) is the wait before a section is read, plus its reading, plus the pass that writes its first token: 0 + 0.2 + 0.01 = 0.21 s. Inter-token latency (ITL) is one writing pass, 10 ms. One section takes TTFT + 999 × ITL = 0.21 + 9.99 = 10.2 s, so 900 one at a time take 9,180 s, 2 h 33 min, 03:30 to 06:03. At 05:00, 5,400 s in, 5,400 ÷ 10.2 = 529 were done. The sheet divided all 3,000 tokens a section by the reading speed: 900 × 3,000 ÷ 10,000 = 270 s. Throughput, tokens a second across all the work, was quoted as one figure and hid two speeds 100 times apart. With one-word grades each section wrote 3 tokens, 0.23 s, 207 s in all, so the sheet stayed close until the report grew to 1,000 tokens. Dead Letter's s9e08 split one answer's wait into the first token and the total; here the same two parts plan a whole job. What can go wrong: a sheet that held for short answers is trusted for long ones.

steps.title: Sending 32 together: one fetch, 32 tokens.
steps.text: First, the script hands the card a group of 32 sections. Second, the card reads all 32 sections' notes; reading already waits on the adders, so it takes 32 × 0.2 = 6.4 s. Third, each writing pass fetches the weights once and adds one token to all 32 reports: 18 ms a pass on the contractor's curve, against 10 ms for one. So the card writes 32 ÷ 0.018 = 1,778 tokens a second instead of 100. 900 sections make 28 groups of 32 (24.4 s each) and one of 4 (0.8 + 11 = 11.8 s): 695 s, 11 min 35 s, done at 03:41:35. Roughly, by hand: 900,000 ÷ 1,778 = 506 s of writing, about 8.5 minutes, plus 180 s of reading, about 3: about 12 minutes. The price: a report's first token now waits for its group's reading, up to 6.42 s, and each pass takes 18 ms instead of 10. The meter: one at a time the card was busy 9,180 s, 2.55 hours; at $2.79 a card hour (one provider's list price) that is $7.11 of card time, against 695 s, about $0.54. What can go wrong: a person waiting on one answer would feel that longer first token.

steps.title: Why the other fixes fall short.
steps.text: Twice the sums a second halves the reading, 0.2 s to 0.1 s, and leaves 10 ms a token: 9,090 s, done at 06:01:30, 90 s saved. Cutting the notes to 500 tokens reads a quarter as much, 0.05 s a section: 9,045 s, done at 06:00:45, 135 s saved, about 2 of the 153 minutes, and the second measurements gone. Grading tonight and writing the reports by day reopens the bridge on time, but the reports reach the owner hours after the contract asks. A bigger model for the reports would fetch more bytes every pass and write each token slower still. What can go wrong: fixing the phase that was already fast.

diagram.aria: Two ways to run the night job on one card. Top row, one at a time: one section's notes, 2,000 tokens; reading, 0.2 s in one pass, waiting on the adders; writing, 1,000 passes of 10 ms, waiting on the road; the report, 10.2 s a section, 100 tokens a second. The job takes 9,180 s and ends at 06:03. Bottom row, 32 together: 32 sections' notes; reading, 6.4 s; writing, 1,000 passes of 18 ms, one fetch giving 32 tokens; 32 reports in 24.4 s, 1,778 tokens a second. 28 groups of 32 and one of 4 take 695 s and end at 03:41:35.

notes.text: One at a time: 900 x 10.2 s = 9,180 s, ends 06:03
32 together: 28 groups and one of 4, 695 s, ends 03:41:35
Reading waits on the adders; writing waits on the road

explain.caption: Read each row left to right. Reading takes a section's 2,000 tokens in one pass and waits on the adders, so 32 sections take 32 times as long. Writing adds one token per pass and waits on the road, so a pass that serves 32 reports costs 18 ms instead of 10: the card writes 1,778 tokens a second instead of 100.

fix.title: The fix: time reading and writing apart, and send 32 sections at once
fix.text: Rebuild the plan sheet with two lines: prompt tokens at the measured reading speed (900 × 2,000 ÷ 10,000 = 180 s) and answer tokens at the measured writing speed for the number of reports in each pass. Set the script to send 32 sections at a time, so each pass fetches the weights once for 32 reports: 18 ms a pass, 1,778 tokens a second, the whole job in 695 s, done at 03:41:35. Before each closure, re-time both speeds on a few real sections, and add a check to the job: if fewer sections are done than the sheet expects at any point, the night lead is told at once, not at 05:00.

limits: The 10,000 tokens a second for reading and the writing curve are the contractor's own measurements on one card and one model. A different card, model or serving program lands elsewhere, so time both phases again after any change.

Larger groups lengthen each report's first token, up to 6.42 s at 32. For a batch job nobody watches that is fine; for a person waiting on one answer, like a6e05's caller waiting for the first word, it is not.
Groups cannot grow without end. Each report in a pass needs room on the card for its working memory, which a later case in this season measures.
explain.seniorTake: A model's work has two phases with two speeds. Reading the prompt (prefill) takes every prompt token in one pass and waits on the card's sums, so it is fast per token: about 10,000 a second here. Writing the answer (decode) adds one token per pass, and every pass fetches every weight, so it waits on memory: about 100 a second for one answer. A single tokens-a-second figure hides that 100-fold gap, and a plan built on it will be right for short answers and badly wrong for long ones, as this sheet was: 270 s planned, 9,180 s taken. Measure time to first token and the time between tokens separately, plan prompt and answer tokens at their own speeds, and then use writing's cheap lever: one fetch of the weights serves every answer in the pass, so 32 at once write 1,778 tokens a second instead of 100. The price is a longer first token per answer, which a batch job can usually afford and a person waiting usually cannot.

realWorld.title: Splitwise: a compute-heavy phase and a memory-heavy one
realWorld.text: Patel and colleagues' Splitwise paper, on serving large language models (LLMs), says there are two main phases during an LLM inference request: a compute-intensive prompt computation, and a memory-intensive token generation. They run the two phases on separate machines, each suited to its phase, and report that we can achieve 1.4x higher throughput at 20% lower cost than current designs. The bridge keeps both phases on one card and plans each at its own speed.

realWorld.title: vLLM: compute-bound prefill, memory-bound decode, and ITL
realWorld.text: vLLM, a widely used open-source serving program, has an Optimization and Tuning page that describes compute-bound (prefill) and memory-bound (decode) operations. On mixing them in one batch it says: It improves inter-token latency (ITL) and generation decode because decode requests are prioritized. And on letting more prompt tokens in at once: Higher values achieve better time to first token (TTFT) as you can process more prefill tokens in a batch. The two clocks pull against each other, as the bridge's longer first token at 32 shows.

realWorld.title: NVIDIA: one vector at a time is memory limited
realWorld.text: NVIDIA's GPU Performance Background User's Guide describes an A100 with up to 2039 GB/s bandwidth from 80 GB of HBM2 memory (high-bandwidth memory stacked beside the chip) and 312 FP16 TFLOPS of dense math (FP16 is 16-bit floating point). It takes a fully-connected layer applied to a single vector, a batch of one, and says it is memory limited. Writing one report at a time is that case; reading 2,000 tokens at once is not.

realWorld.title: What an hour of the card costs
realWorld.text: The contractor owns its card, but the meter is easier to read in rent. Lambda's pricing page, read on 16 October 2026, lists NVIDIA A100 SXM 80 GB (SXM is the board form the card is built in) at $2.79 a GPU an hour. At that price the night's job cost $7.11 of card time one at a time and about $0.54 sent 32 at once. Prices change; the arithmetic is the lesson.

asked: What are prefill and decode, and why do they run at different speeds?
How would you estimate the time for a 900-document generation job?
interview.answer: Prefill is reading the prompt: the model takes in every prompt token in one pass, so each weight fetched from memory is used for all of them, and the job is limited by the card's compute. Decode is writing the answer: one token per pass, and each pass fetches every weight again, so it is limited by memory bandwidth while the compute mostly waits. On one A100 with an 8-billion-weight model in 16 bits, that came to about 10,000 prompt tokens a second against about 100 answer tokens a second for one answer. To estimate a 900-document job, I'd measure both speeds on a few real documents, then add them up separately: prompt tokens at the prefill speed, plus answer tokens at the decode speed for the number of answers sharing each pass. Each answer takes its time to first token plus one inter-token gap for every token after the first. I once saw a sheet that divided all tokens by the prefill speed: it said 270 s, and one at a time the job took 9,180 s, because each 1,000-token answer needed 1,000 passes of about 10 ms. Then I'd batch: one fetch of the weights serves every answer in the pass, so 32 answers at 18 ms a pass write about 1,778 tokens a second, and that job fell to about 12 minutes. I'd check the trade too: batching lengthens each answer's time to first token, which is fine for an overnight job and not for a chat.

terms.def: A bridge whose road deck hangs from two great cables slung between towers. The Strathcarne Bridge closes one night a month for inspection.
The upright cables that hold the road deck up from a suspension bridge's two main cables.
The person who runs the inspection team through the night and answers for its work. Omolara is the contractor's.
An inspector who works hanging from ropes to reach the deck's underside, the cables and the towers.
A small remote-controlled flying machine with a camera. It photographs parts of the bridge the inspectors can't reach.
One numbered stretch of deck or cable checked on the night. There are 900, each with about 2,000 tokens of notes.
What the inspectors and the drone record for a section: measurements, cracks, wear. About 2,000 tokens each; the model reads them first.
The one-word rating the job wrote for each section until tonight, such as sound or watch: 3 tokens, 0.23 s a section.
The full write-up of one section, about 1,000 tokens, that the new contract asks for by reopening. It takes 10.2 s one at a time.
The owner's engineer who decides whether the bridge reopens. Kristiina reads every section graded watch or worse first.
The owner's agreement with the inspection firm. From 8 September 2026 it asks for a full report per section, ready by reopening.
Hildebrand's page of how long the job takes: 900 × 3,000 tokens ÷ 10,000 a second = 270 s. It used one speed for every token.
The small program that feeds sections to the card and collects the reports. Tonight it sent one section at a time.
The script's record: for each section, the time, its reading, the wait for its first token, the gap between tokens and the whole section.
A program that writes text one small piece at a time, having learned from huge amounts of text (a1e01).
A small piece of text, often part of a word, that a model reads and writes (a1e03). A section's notes are about 2,000; a report about 1,000.
The learned numbers a model is made of (a1e02). Llama 3.1 8B has 8.03 billion, 16.06 billion bytes in 16 bits.
A unit of computer storage, 8 bits. Each weight here takes 2 bytes.
Meta's open-weights language model with 8.03 billion weights (a10e01). In 16 bits its file is 16.06 billion bytes, about 15 GB on the card's meter.
A board with a GPU, a graphics processing unit, and its memory: thousands of small adders fed by one fast memory road (a10e01). The contractor owns one A100 80GB.
Short for graphics processing unit, the chip on a graphics card that does the sums.
This season's word for the card's many small units that do sums, all at once. Reading waits on them.
This season's word for the link that carries numbers from the card's memory to its adders: 2,039 GB/s on the A100. Writing waits on it.
Gigabyte, about a billion bytes. Memory speeds use the maker's 1,000 (2,039 GB/s); the card's meter counts 1 GB as 1,024 MB.
How many multiplications or additions the adders can do each second. The A100's sheet says 312 trillion, 312 TFLOPS.
Short for trillion floating-point operations per second: sums a second on numbers with a decimal point. The A100: 312 (16-bit, dense).
One trip of the card through the whole model. Reading takes all of a section's tokens in one pass; writing adds one token per pass.
The first phase: the card takes in all 2,000 tokens of a section's notes in one pass, like a letter at a glance. 0.2 s here, about 10,000 tokens a second.
The second phase: one token per pass, each pass fetching every weight, like writing a reply one word at a time. About 10 ms a token here.
The engineers' name for reading the prompt. It is math limited and fast per token.
The engineers' name for writing the answer, one token per pass. It is memory limited and slow per token.
The text a model is given to read before it writes (a2e01): here a section's notes, about 2,000 tokens.
A millisecond, a thousandth of a second. A writing pass takes about 10 ms, a hundredth of a second.
The wait from sending a request until its first token arrives (a2e07, a6e05): here the wait, the reading and one pass, 0.21 s one at a time.
The gap between one token and the next: one writing pass. 10 ms for one report, 18 ms when 32 share each pass.
Tokens a second across all the card's work. Writing one report: 100; 32 at once: 1,778. One figure can hide two speeds.
The contractor's own timing of its A100: a pass takes 10 ms plus 0.25 ms per report in it, rounded here to whole ms. 1: 10 ms, 8: 12, 32: 18.
Sections sent to the card together. Their notes are read, then every pass adds one token to each report. Also called a batch.
Waiting on the adders, because each byte fetched is used for many sums. Reading a 2,000-token section is math limited (compute-bound).
Waiting on the memory road, because each byte fetched is used for about one sum. Writing one report is memory limited (memory-bound).
How many sums a job does with each byte it fetches. Writing one report: about 1. The A100 could do about 153 (312 ÷ 2.039).
How long the job holds the card: 9,180 s one at a time, 695 s at 32. At a rented $2.79 an hour: $7.11 against $0.54.
The job's screen of sections done out of 900. At 05:00 it said 529.
The international standard for information security management. Its Annex A control 8.6 covers capacity management.
Making sure systems have the resources the work needs, now and later, by monitoring, testing and planning.

atWork: Look for a batch generation job, a run that writes many answers overnight or on a schedule, planned with one tokens-a-second figure. It is a common pattern: the plan works for short answers, the answers grow, and the job misses its window by hours. Ask four things. What are the reading and writing speeds, measured separately on your own prompts and answers? How many prompt tokens and how many answer tokens does the job have, each at its own speed? How many answers share each writing pass, and what does that do to the time to first token? And does the job warn someone when it falls behind its plan, before the deadline? A later build project will ask you to measure this. Standards-readiness note, stated conditionally and not legal advice: if your organisation is certified to ISO/IEC 27001:2022 or working toward it, an auditor checking Annex A 8.6 (capacity management, as summarised by a third-party guide) would look for a job plan built from measured reading and writing speeds, re-measured after changes, with monitoring that shows when the job falls behind.

recall.prompt: An insurer plans a night job on one card: 400 claim files, each about 6,000 tokens to take in and a 500-token summary to put out. Its sheet says 400 × 6,500 ÷ 10,000 = 260 s, from the 10,000 tokens a second it measured. The job log shows each file's text taken in at that rate, and the summaries coming out at about 100 tokens a second. What do you tell them?

keyIdeas.idea: The 10,000 is the reading (prefill) speed, all of a file's tokens in one pass; writing (decode) is one token per pass, about 100 a second
Sum each phase at its own speed: 0.6 s of reading and 5 s of writing a file, 5.6 s, about 37 minutes one at a time
Send many files together: one fetch of the weights per pass serves every summary in it

recall.model: Their 10,000 tokens a second is the reading speed, prefill: the card takes in all of a file's tokens in one pass. Writing, decode, adds one token per pass at about 100 a second, so the two speeds are 100 times apart. Per file: 6,000 ÷ 10,000 = 0.6 s of reading and 500 tokens at about 10 ms each, 5 s of writing, 5.6 s; one at a time, 400 × 5.6 = 2,240 s, about 37 minutes, not 260 s. Plan each phase at its own speed, then send files together: each pass fetches the weights once and adds a token to every summary in it, so a batch of 32 writes far more tokens a second.

recall.prompt: A section's first token arrives after 0.21 s, and each token after it comes 10 ms later. How long does its 1,000-token report take?
recall.why: TTFT + 999 × ITL = 0.21 + 999 × 0.01 = 10.2 s. 0.3 s is 3,000 tokens at the reading speed, the plan sheet's mistake: it timed the writing as if it were reading.

recall.prompt: In an interview you're asked: what are prefill and decode, and why do they run at different speeds?

keyIdeas.idea: Prefill reads the whole prompt in one pass, using each fetched weight for every prompt token, so it is limited by the sums (compute)
Decode writes one token per pass and fetches every weight each time, so it is limited by memory bandwidth
So time to first token and the time between tokens are measured and planned separately

recall.model: Prefill is reading the prompt: the card takes in every prompt token in one pass, so each weight it fetches is used for all of them, and the job is limited by its sums a second, its compute. Decode is writing: one token per pass, and each pass fetches every weight from memory, so it is limited by memory bandwidth while the adders mostly wait. On an A100 with an 8-billion-weight model, reading ran at about 10,000 tokens a second and writing at about 100. So I measure time to first token (TTFT) and the time between tokens (ITL) separately, and plan prompt tokens and answer tokens at their own speeds.

recall.prompt: 32 reports share each writing pass, and a pass takes 18 ms. About how many tokens a second does the card write in all?
recall.why: Each pass adds one token to each of 32 reports: 32 ÷ 0.018 = 1,778 a second. One report on its own gets 1,000 ÷ 18 = 56 a second, but the card writes 1,778 in all, against 100 when it writes one report at a time.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 4 months later. Since October the plan sheet has two lines, reading and writing, and the script sends 32 sections at a time. The October, November and December jobs each finished at 03:41, and the bridge reopened at 05:30 every time. In December the owner asked for longer reports from the next closure, in January: about 2,000 tokens a section, with a repair estimate in each. Hildebrand's new sheet says twice the tokens out means twice the job: 23 minutes. Same notes, same card, same groups of 32.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Is Hildebrand right that the January job takes twice as long? What grows, what doesn't, and about how long will it take?

keyIdeas.idea: Reading the notes doesn't change: still 0.2 s a section, about 3 minutes in all
Only the writing doubles: 1.8 million tokens at 1,778 a second, about 17 minutes (2,000 passes of 18 ms, 36 s a group)
About 20 minutes in all, done by about 03:50, well before 05:30

coldCase.model: Not quite. Only the writing doubles. Each group of 32 still reads its notes in 6.4 s, so reading stays at about 3 minutes for all 900 sections (900 × 0.2 s = 180 s). Writing doubles: 2,000 passes of 18 ms is 36 s a group instead of 18, or 1.8 million tokens at 1,778 a second, about 17 minutes. By hand that is about 20 minutes; group by group, 28 × (6.4 + 36) + (0.8 + 22) = 1,210 s, 20 min 10 s, done at 03:50:10, well before 05:30. The sheet should keep its two lines and double only the writing one. One caution belongs on it too: a longer answer makes each pass also fetch more of the model's working memory for that answer, the next case's subject, so the 18 ms a pass should be measured again before January rather than assumed.
